extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology/psychoanalysis and researchers of humor and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting psychoanalytic criteria for what produces humorous effect: mechanisms, conditions, and forms of humor as described by Freud (economy of affect, displacement, relation to wit and the comic). Useful for analyzing or producing humor from a psychoanalytic/theoretical perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as economy in expenditure of affect
rubrics_metrics.description: "The pleasure of humor results at the cost of this discontinued liberation of affect; it originates through the _economized expenditure of affect_."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core formula: humor converts affect which would otherwise be expended (pity, anger, fear, etc.) into pleasure by withholding the expected affective discharge. Examples: a disinterested observer laughs because the emotional expenditure (pity) prepared in him becomes inapplicable; Mark Twain stories exemplify diverting sympathy into humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for humor: suppression of painful affects 'statu nascendi'
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor requires that when a situation tempts us to release painful affects, motives urge us to suppress these affects _statu nascendi_ (at the moment of arising), creating conditions for humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion for humor-production: present a situation that would normally elicit painful affect, then show or imply a withholding of that affect so the observer experiences a pleasurable substitution. Anti-pattern: if the audience is personally affected or cannot defend against the pain, comic effect is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor can be self-sufficient in a single person
rubrics_metrics.description: "Humor is the most self-sufficient of the forms of the comic; its process consummating itself in one single person and the participation of another adds nothing new to it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humoristic pleasure may be produced and enjoyed internally by the humorist without needing to impart it. However, sympathetic understanding by others can reproduce the same pleasure (the audience entering into the producer's psychic processes). Example: grim-humor of condemned criminals: the humor is internal but can infect observers who understand the indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of sympathy as a frequent source of humoristic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: One common mechanism is economizing sympathy: diverting or inhibiting the sympathetic expenditure (pity) that would normally arise, thereby producing laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mark Twain stories where sympathy is deflected (e.g., focusing on loss of half-day's pay rather than injury) so audience's pity is inhibited and replaced by humor. Use narrative emphasis on trivializing or reframing the expected sympathetic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of humor determined by which affect is economized
rubrics_metrics.description: "The forms of humor are extraordinarily varied according to the nature of the emotional feelings which are economized in favor of humor, as sympathy, anger, pain, compassion, etc."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create varied humor, artists can target different affective systems (anger, fear, disgust, compassion) and find techniques to withhold or redirect those specific affect-discharges. Creative expansion occurs when writers master humoristic handling of previously unconquered affects (e.g., fear, disgust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor may fuse with wit or other comic forms to remove obstructive emotional development
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can appear fused with wit or any other form of the comic, where it is entrusted with the task of removing a possible emotional development which would form a hindrance to pleasurable effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blended techniques: use humoristic elements to neutralize an affect that would otherwise block comic appreciation (e.g., a witticism that also dampens pity). Partial setting aside of affect is more common than complete: 'broken' humor that 'smiles under its tears' is typical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humoristic displacement as a defense-like mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Humoristic displacement resembles psychological defense processes: it withdraws the energy reserved for a painful affect and redirects it into pleasure rather than repressing the idea; Freud calls humor a lofty variant of defense activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism guidance: craft humor so that the expected affective release is deflected to secondary or peripheral matters (displacement), allowing the latent painful idea to remain conscious yet transformed into pleasure. Connection to infancy: childhood affective experiences supply the material enabling such revaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization in the foreconscious / requirement of automatic (non-conscious) processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor, like the comic, is psychically localized in the foreconscious; the humoristic displacement is impossible under conscious attention and requires automatic/foreconscious processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: attempts to produce humor by explicit, reflective explanation ('philosophic thinking') will fail to generate humoristic pleasure. Effective humor should operate via automatic, not deliberative, mental routes—allowing the audience to experience the displacement without conscious calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of humor from wit and the comic (three economy-formulae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud's summary formula: wit originates from an "economy of expenditure in inhibition," the comic from an "economy of expenditure in thought," and humor from an "economy of expenditure in feeling."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this triad to analyze or design material: if the effect aims at relieving inhibitory effort (wit), at mental shortcuts/comparisons (comic), or at withheld affective discharge (humor), choose techniques accordingly. Example: wordplay often produces wit (inhibition economy); juxtaposition of two thought-modes produces comic (thought economy); emotional reframing produces humor (feeling economy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor is generally closer to the comic than to wit, but differs in mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor shares localization with the comic (foreconscious) and differs from wit (compromise between unconscious and foreconscious). The comic requires applying two different modes of ideas to the same thought-function (comparison), whereas humor is characterized by the evasion or inhibition of an expected emotional development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic distinction: do not conflate humor with wit; determine whether pleasure arises from cognitive comparison (comic), unconscious-foreconscious juxtaposition (wit), or affective withholding (humor). Techniques effective for comic (sudden conceptual comparison) may not suffice for humor, which needs affective context and withholding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-state constraints: personal involvement, admiration, or empathy can inhibit humor
rubrics_metrics.description: If the hearer is personally affected by the painful emotion or admires the humoristic person, the humoristic pleasure may be inhibited (e.g., admiration covering the humoristic pleasure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing humor about suffering or noble behavior, be aware that admiration or direct personal involvement can suppress laughter. Effective humor often presumes a degree of disinterest or distance in the audience; lack of this distance is an anti-pattern for humoristic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of repetition and expectation management in producing humoristic/comic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition can produce comical effect through monotony and the buildup of expectation (example: the cow falling through forty-six nights until the brother remarks 'beginning to grow monotonous'), leading to humor when the audience's expected emotional response is subverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: cultivate repetition and delay of the expected affective reaction; the eventual unexpected or understated response (e.g., indifference, trivialization) converts anticipated affect into humor. Beware: repetition alone may create monotony unless coupled with a displacement or withholding that reframes the affect.
